en: The Philippine eagle, our national bird, has specialized crown feathers called a crest that it can raise or lower to communicate in the dense rainforest canopy.
The sampaguita, our national flower, releases its strongest sweet fragrance at night to attract specific moth pollinators in the local environment.
The Ifugao rice terraces use a traditional stone-wall irrigation system that naturally filters and distributes gravity-fed mountain spring water to each flooded paddy.
Filipino scientist Ramon Barba invented a potassium nitrate spray that safely triggers mango trees to flower out of season, boosting local harvests.
The narra, our national tree, produces highly durable, termite-resistant heartwood because it naturally accumulates dense extractives and silica as it matures.
T'boli weavers extract abaca fibers by manually scraping the stalk's pseudostem, relying on the plant's naturally long and strong cellulose fibers.
Exiled in Dapitan, Jose Rizal applied his scientific knowledge to build a gravity-driven water system using local clay, stones, and bamboo pipes.
The carabao, our national animal, wallows in mud to cool its body because it lacks sufficient sweat glands for effective thermoregulation.
Mayon Volcano's perfect conical shape results from repeated, highly viscous lava flows cooling and solidifying around its central vent over centuries.
Indigenous artisans create vibrant traditional textiles by boiling local plants like indigo and turmeric to extract stable, colorfast natural pigments.
The bangus, our national fish, has specialized pharyngeal teeth and a long intestine to efficiently digest the algae and detritus it eats.
Filipino physicist Gregorio Zara discovered the "Zara effect," which describes how electrical resistance increases when two sliding metal contacts separate.
